images.filename: Charles-Gédéon Giasson & Agathe Macomber, full picture.gif
images.caption: Charles-Gédéon Giasson et Agathe McComber, de Kahnawake. Charles-Giasson and Agathe McComber married in 1832. They lived in Kahnawake and had many children including Léon-Trefflé Akiohanes Giasson and Napoléon-Antoine Giasson. The first married Agnès Brault in 1886 and the second married Marguerite Meunier dite Lafleur in 1875. Agathe McComber died in 1889 at the age of eighty-one. Interestingly, the attorney hired by the Giasson family to prevent their planned eviction in the late 1800s was Albert-Emmanuel de Lorimier, a son of controversial George de Lorimier (see other pictures). Albert-E. de Lorimier eventually obtained for the Giasson's their right to remain in Kahnawake.

images.caption: Photograph / sketch of Claude-Nicolas-Guillaume de Lorimier. Claude-Nicolas-Guillaume de Lorimier (1744-1825) was also known as Major de Lorimier or Teiohatekon. He is the father of George de Lorimier and a key source of the antagonism that was felt toward his son and other so-called 'white' Kahnawake residents in the nineteenth century. He and his twelve children descended from a French military family. In 1783, following his service during the American Revolution as one of the officers of British Indian warriors, he married an Iroquois woman by the name of Marie-Louise Schuyler and the couple moved to Kahnawake, where he became resident agent. In 1801, after the deaths of his first two wives, the second of which was white, Claude married Iroquois Anne Skaouennetsi (also known as Anne McGregor or Anne Gregory) with whom he had four children, including George de Lorimier. After the War of 1812, he gradually retired from military life. He remained in Kahnawake until his death in 1825

images.filename: Twin railway lift bridges over St. Lawrence Seaway in Montreal.jpg
images.caption: A side-by-side pair of identical vertical-lift bridges in Greater Montreal, Quebec, Canada, carrying a double-track rail line over the St. Lawrence Seaway.  More specifically, the location is in Kahnawake, just across from the city of Montreal proper.  The twin lift bridges over the Seaway are on the same rail line as the Saint-Laurent Railway Bridge, which crosses the St. Lawrence River, and are only about 1,200 feet (370 m) south of that longer bridge.  In the background (to the east) is the southern section of the Mercier Bridge (road bridge on Quebec Route 138).
